detail: A Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation is the most common form of company insolvency in the UK.
verified_quote: In 2025 CVLs were the most common company insolvency procedure (77%), followed by compulsory liquidations (16%), administrations (6%) and CVAs (1%), whilst receivership appointments made up less than 1% of cases.
notes: This data is for England and Wales in 2025, according to The Insolvency Service official statistics published on GOV.UK. Similar trends are reported for January 2026 and for Scotland since April 2020.

detail: Shareholders can shorten the 14 days' notice for a special resolution to wind up the company to 7 days if 90% of shareholders agree.
verified_quote: A general meeting may be called by shorter notice than that specified in subsection (1) or (2) if it is agreed by a majority in number of the members having a right to attend and vote at the meeting, being a majority together holding not less than 90% in nominal value of the shares giving that right (or, in the case of a company not having a share capital, together representing not less than 90% of the total voting rights at the meeting).
notes: The Companies Act 2006, Section 307(4) states that a general meeting (where a special resolution to wind up the company would be passed) can be called with 'shorter notice' than the statutory 14 days for private companies, provided a majority of members representing not less than 90% of the total voting rights agree. However, the legislation or official GOV.UK guidance does not explicitly specify that this shortened period is exactly '7 days'. The term used is 'shorter notice'.

detail: Creditors must receive at least 7 days' notice of the proposed liquidation and decision procedure.
verified_quote: Notices of decision procedures, and notices seeking deemed consent, must be delivered in accordance with the following table: ... creditors' voluntary winding up, decisions of creditors for appointment of liquidator ... Minimum notice required: ... in other cases, 3 business days.
notes: Rule 15.11(1) of The Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016 specifies different minimum notice periods for decision procedures in creditors' voluntary winding up, depending on the circumstances. While 14 days and 7 days are applicable in certain conversion scenarios, 'in other cases' (which would cover a standard CVL) the minimum notice required for decisions of creditors for the appointment of a liquidator is 3 business days. This contradicts the claim that creditors must receive at least 7 days' notice.

detail: A physical meeting of creditors is only held if requested by 10% of creditors by value or number, or by 10 individual creditors.
verified_quote: A physical creditors' meeting may only be called if, after notice of a decision making process has been sent to creditors, more than 10% in number or value of creditors or more than 10 creditors in actual number request a physical meeting.
notes: This is stipulated in the Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016, Rule 15.6, which refers to the thresholds in sections 246ZE(7) and 379ZA(7) of the Insolvency Act 1986, introduced by the Small Business Enterprise and Employment Act 2015. The quoted text is from official guidance on the Insolvency Rules 2016.

detail: If creditors nominate a different liquidator, their nomination usually overrides that of the shareholders.
The liquidator is required to advertise their appointment in The Gazette.
verified_quote: Section 109 of the Insolvency Act 1986 requires a liquidator, within 14 days of appointment, to notify the Registrar of Companies, and to publish a notice of appointment in the Gazette using forms 600 and 600a, as specified by the Companies (Forms) (Amendments) Regulations 1987.
notes: The requirement for a liquidator to advertise their appointment in The Gazette is mandated by Section 109 of the Insolvency Act 1986. This is confirmed by official guidance from The Insolvency Service. The Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016 (Rule 6.23(1)) refers to the notice of appointment in accordance with section 109(1). Companies House also provides forms (e.g., Form 600a) for this purpose for voluntary liquidations (including Creditors' Voluntary Liquidations) for insertion in The Gazette.

detail: A liquidator can seek a court order for a director to repay, restore, or account for money or property if they are found guilty of misfeasance (a breach of duty, such as misapplying company money/property, or breach of fiduciary duty).
verified_quote: The court may, on the application of the official receiver or the liquidator, ... examine into the conduct of the person falling within subsection (1) and compel him— (a) to repay, restore or account for the money or property or any part of it, with interest at such rate as the court thinks just, or (b) to contribute such sum to the company’s assets by way of compensation in respect of the misfeasance or breach of fiduciary or other duty as the court thinks just.
notes: The claim is directly verified by Section 212 of the Insolvency Act 1986. Subsection (1) defines the circumstances, including misapplying or retaining company money/property, or being guilty of misfeasance or breach of any fiduciary or other duty. Subsection (3) empowers the court, on application by a liquidator, to compel the individual to repay, restore, or account for the money or property, or to contribute a sum as compensation. The version of the Act is in force, with no relevant changes affecting this specific claim noted up to 04 June 2026.

detail: The Rating (Coronavirus) and Directors Disqualification (Dissolved Companies) Act, introduced in December 2021, extended the Insolvency Service's powers to investigate and disqualify directors of dissolved companies retrospectively for up to 15 years, and the Business Secretary can apply for compensation orders.
card_name: Rating (Coronavirus) and Directors Disqualification (Dissolved Companies) Act
verified_quote: The Rating (Coronavirus) and Directors Disqualification (Dissolved Companies) Act 2021 extended the provision to include directors of dissolved companies. This provision is retrospective which means that conduct before the Act came into force can be taken into account. The Insolvency Service can apply to the court for a compensation order on behalf of the Secretary of State for Business & Trade.
notes: The Rating (Coronavirus) and Directors Disqualification (Dissolved Companies) Act 2021 received Royal Assent on 15th December 2021. This Act amended the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986, which allows for disqualification orders ranging from 2 to 15 years. The extended powers therefore include disqualification for up to 15 years.

detail: Breach of Section 216 of the Insolvency Act 1986 (restrictions on reusing company names) is a criminal offence, punishable by imprisonment of up to two years and/or a fine, and can also make the director personally liable for the debts of the new company incurred while using the prohibited name.
verified_quote: If you are found in breach of these restrictions you could be: prosecuted and, if convicted, imprisoned and/or fined, and sometimes an order to confiscate the proceeds of crime will be made; made personally liable for the debts incurred by the company during the breach.
notes: Section 216(4) of the Insolvency Act 1986 states that a person contravening the section is liable to imprisonment or a fine, or both. Schedule 10 of the Insolvency Act 1986 specifies that for contravening restrictions on the re-use of a company name in insolvent liquidation, the punishment on indictment is 2 years imprisonment or a fine, or both. Personal liability for debts incurred by the new company is further detailed in Section 217 of the Insolvency Act 1986.

detail: HMRC's preferential creditor status was introduced by the Finance Act 2020.
verified_quote: In Schedule 6 to that Act (preferential debts) after paragraph 15C insert—. Category 9: Certain HMRC debts. 15D(1)Any amount owed at the relevant date by the debtor to the Commissioners in respect of—. (a)value added tax, or. (b)a relevant deduction.
notes: HMRC's secondary preferential creditor status was introduced by the Finance Act 2020, specifically Section 98, which amended Schedule 6 of the Insolvency Act 1986. The changes took effect for insolvencies commencing on or after 1 December 2020. This status applies to certain taxes collected by businesses on behalf of others, such as VAT, PAYE, and employee National Insurance contributions.

detail: HMRC's secondary preferential creditor status applies to PAYE, VAT, employee National Insurance Contributions, student loan repayments, and Construction Industry Scheme deductions.
verified_quote: From 1 December 2020, once ordinary preferential creditors have been paid, HMRC will be a secondary preferential creditor for taxes held on behalf of employees and customers. These changes only apply to VAT and CIS, employee NICs, PAYE and student loan deductions.
notes: HMRC's secondary preferential creditor status, introduced by the Finance Act 2020, applies to insolvencies commencing on or after 1 December 2020. The specific deductions are clarified in The Insolvency Act 1986 (HMRC Debts: Priority on Insolvency) Regulations 2020.

detail: HMRC can issue Personal Liability Notices (PLNs) under the Social Security Administration Act 1998 to make directors personally liable for unpaid PAYE and National Insurance Contributions (NICs) if the failure to pay was due to the director's fraud or neglect.
verified_quote: This section applies to contributions which a body corporate is liable to pay, where— (a)the body corporate has failed to pay the contributions at or within the time prescribed for the purpose; and (b)the failure appears to the [F2Inland Revenue] to be attributable to fraud or neglect on the part of one or more individuals who, at the time of the fraud or neglect, were officers of the body corporate (“culpable officers”).
notes: The power for HMRC to issue Personal Liability Notices (PLNs) to make directors personally liable for unpaid National Insurance Contributions (NICs) due to fraud or neglect is indeed found in Section 121C of the Social Security Administration Act 1992. While the claim refers to the Social Security Administration Act 1998, this Act, specifically Section 64, introduced the PLN mechanism and came into effect on 6 April 2009, making amendments to the Social Security Administration Act 1992 to insert Section 121C. Therefore, the originating legislative event for the PLN was the 1998 Act, but the specific power resides within the 1992 Act. HMRC's guidance consistently refers to Section 121C of the Social Security Administration Act 1992 in relation to NICs. However, the claim's inclusion of PAYE alongside NICs as being covered by this specific PLN under the Social Security Administration Act is not directly supported by the text of Section 121C itself, which refers to 'contributions' (understood as NICs), or by HMRC's specific guidance on this section. Other statutory provisions may cover personal liability for PAYE, but not under this specific PLN as stated in the claim.

detail: The liquidator's post-appointment fees can be calculated as a percentage of realised assets, based on time spent, or a set amount.
verified_quote: An administrator, liquidator or trustee in bankruptcy is entitled to receive remuneration for services as office-holder. The remuneration may be fixed (a) as a percentage of the value of the assets which are realised or distributed or both, or (b) by reference to the time properly given by the office-holder and the office-holder's staff in attending to matters arising in the insolvency, or (c) as a set amount.
notes: This is from Rule 18.16(1) and (2) of The Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016, which came into force on 6th April 2017.

detail: Occasional creditor contributions may be considered in rare circumstances to help cover liquidation costs.
verified_quote: All fees, costs, charges and other expenses incurred in the course of the winding up are to be treated as expenses of the winding up. The expenses of the winding up are payable out of— (a) assets of the company available for the payment of general creditors, including— (i) proceeds of any legal action which the liquidator has power to bring in the liquidator's own name or in the name of the company, (ii) proceeds arising from any award made under any arbitration or other dispute resolution procedure which the liquidator has power to bring in the liquidator's own name or in the name of the company (b) subject as provided in rules 6.44 to 6.48, property comprised in or subject to a floating charge created by the company.
notes: Rule 6.42 of The Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016 (in force) clearly states that the expenses of a Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation are payable out of the company's assets. There is no provision in authoritative UK legislation or official guidance for creditors to make contributions to cover liquidation costs. The general principle from official guidance is that liquidation costs are paid from the company's assets.

detail: Directors are eligible for redundancy pay if they worked at least 16 hours per week and were employed for a minimum of two years, with payments being part of a government-backed scheme.
verified_quote: Removal of 'you worked a minimum of 16 hours per week' from criteria that must be met for us to consider a claim.
notes: Directors are eligible for redundancy pay if they can demonstrate they were also employees of the company. The requirement for directors to have worked a minimum of 16 hours per week was removed from the Insolvency Service's criteria for considering a claim on 30 September 2022. However, to qualify for statutory redundancy pay, an employee (including a director acting as an employee) must generally have been employed for a minimum of two years. Payments are part of a government-backed scheme, administered by the Redundancy Payments Service (part of the Insolvency Service) from the National Insurance Fund.
